context_blurb:
Every person begins as one cell, made when a sperm and an egg fuse. Meiosis, the division that makes those sex cells, explains how traits reshuffle, why blood must be matched for a transfusion, and why some illnesses strike mostly men.

A chromosome is a strand of DNA carrying genes; a gene's versions are its alleles. Human body cells hold 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent. Meiosis divides twice, leaving each sex cell one set of 23, and August Weismann saw why. Halving keeps the count from doubling every generation: if eggs and sperm kept all 46, a child's first cell would hold 92.

In the first division the partners of each pair line up side by side and part, each pair facing either way at random. So each of a woman's eggs gets a chance mix of chromosomes from her mother and her father, every pair sorting on its own: over eight million possible mixes. This is independent assortment.

In 1911 Thomas Hunt Morgan found two genes on a fruit fly's X chromosome, for white eyes and miniature wings, linked: inherited together far more often than chance predicts. Yet some young broke the pair. Morgan proposed crossing over: paired chromosomes, lying side by side, break and swap matching pieces, so a white-eye gene can land beside a normal-wing gene.

Morgan's student Alfred Sturtevant skipped his homework one night to draw the first gene map. Crossing over splits genes far apart more often, since more swap points lie between them, so he read that percentage as distance. For three genes, the outer pair's figure nearly equalled the inner two added. Distances add like that only along a line, so the genes lie in a line, each in a fixed place, like beads on a string.

Gregor Mendel had seen independent sorting in peas, crossing round yellow with wrinkled green, round and yellow being dominant, and letting the offspring self-pollinate. Round is three chances in four and green one in four, so round with green is a quarter of three quarters, about three in sixteen; Mendel counted 108 of 556. Genes close together on one chromosome seldom part, so they give only a few new mixes.

Some alleles do not mask their partners. A pure-breeding red snapdragon crossed with a white one gives pink offspring: incomplete dominance. Cross two pinks, and since each parent hands on red or white by chance, the seedlings come out about one red to two pink to one white. Red and white return because the alleles never blended.

Around 1900 Karl Landsteiner mixed his colleagues' serum, the liquid part of blood, with one another's red cells. Some mixes clumped, as serum's antibodies attack foreign markers: group A serum attacks the B marker, group B serum the A. His students Adriano Sturli and Alfred von Decastello found rare cells clumped by both. Those cells carried both the A marker and the B marker, so the group was named AB; group O cells carry neither. In an AB person each allele makes its marker in full: codominance.

Emil von Dungern and Ludwik Hirszfeld, having shown the groups are inherited, proposed two genes: A or no A, and B or no B. In 1924 Felix Bernstein proposed one gene with three alleles, O, A and B. Most families fit both. The telling case is an AB parent: under two genes, such a parent could pass on a no-A and a no-B copy together, making a group O child possible; Bernstein's AB parent has only A and B to give. Families bore Bernstein out.

The genes for the eye's red-sensing and green-sensing pigments lie on the X chromosome, of which a man has one and a woman two. One faulty copy on a man's single X makes him colour-blind, but a woman needs the faulty gene on both of her X chromosomes, because one working copy is usually enough. John Dalton's preserved eye, studied in the 1990s, lacked the green-pigment gene.

Queen Victoria never had haemophilia, in which blood fails to clot, and no case is known before her; yet her son Leopold did, and two daughters without signs, Alice and Beatrice, had sons who did. Victoria carried the faulty gene on one of her X chromosomes, so each child had an even chance of getting it: a son who did was ill, a daughter a carrier. Prince Albert could not have given it to Leopold: a father gives his sons his Y.
